name: Boboniu and Jianghu
description: Since Boboniu finished building his Jianghu, he has been doing Kungfu on these mountains every day. Boboniu designs a map for his $$$n$$$ mountains. He uses $$$n-1$$$ roads to connect all $$$n$$$ mountains. Every pair of mountains is connected via roads. For the $$$i$$$-th mountain, Boboniu estimated the tiredness of doing Kungfu on the top of it as $$$t_i$$$. He also estimated the height of each mountain as $$$h_i$$$. A path is a sequence of mountains $$$M$$$ such that for each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \lt |M|$$$), there exists a road between $$$M_i$$$ and $$$M_{i+1}$$$. Boboniu would regard the path as a challenge if for each $$$i$$$ ($$$1\le i \lt |M|$$$), $$$h_{M_i}\le h_{M_{i+1}}$$$. Boboniu wants to divide all $$$n-1$$$ roads into several challenges . Note that each road must appear in exactly one challenge, but a mountain may appear in several challenges. Boboniu wants to minimize the total tiredness to do all the challenges . The tiredness of a challenge $$$M$$$ is the sum of tiredness of all mountains in it, i.e. $$$\sum_{i=1}^{|M|}t_{M_i}$$$. He asked you to find the minimum total tiredness. As a reward for your work, you'll become a guardian in his Jianghu.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$), denoting the number of the mountains. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n$$$ ($$$1 \le t_i \le 10^6$$$), denoting the tiredness for Boboniu to do Kungfu on each mountain. The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n$$$ ($$$1 \le h_i \le 10^6$$$), denoting the height of each mountain. Each of the following $$$n - 1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u_i$$$, $$$v_i$$$ ($$$1 \le u_i, v_i \le n, u_i \neq v_i$$$), denoting the ends of the road. It's guaranteed that all mountains are connected via roads.
output_specification: Print one integer: the smallest sum of tiredness of all challenges.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1394D — Boboniu and Jianghu [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
